Yesterday we learned that a judge allowed a $32 billion lawsuit to proceed, accusing Apple's Photos face recognition feature of violating state privacy laws.

While the two companies sit at opposite ends of the privacy spectrum, this case has been conflated with Meta's use of face recognition. The court allowed it to proceed without understanding how the feature works…

Earlier Meta accusations

To properly understand this situation, we need to start with a face recognition lawsuit against Meta that goes back to 2015.

Since the face recognition was performed on Meta's servers, and Meta could identify those faces, the company was indeed breaking the law, and ultimately had to settle for $650 million.

Apple is now being sued under the same Illinois law — the Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) — which says companies can't collect biometric data without consent.

Apple does it very differently

There's an obvious problem with this accusation: Apple absolutely did not collect biometric data to do face recognition in its Photos app. As the company pointed out in a 2021 machine learning research paper, the recognition algorithms run entirely on-device.

And all the iPhone does is tell the user, "these photos look like they are of the same person" — it has no idea who that person is. Only the iPhone user can give them a name.

The company's Photos privacy document reflects this as well.

This lawsuit has been winding its way through the justice system for six years, and now it's just absurd, because a few minutes of research would show the lawsuit's accusations are clearly wrong.

The courts and legislators should be actively praising Apple for its approach to privacy, not conflating it with the privacy-destroying approach of companies like Meta.

This is yet another example of the courts and legislators fundamentally not understanding the technology they're trying to regulate. Of course, the best example is with end-to-end encryption. Multiple countries have threatened or tried to ban end-to-end encryption, without any understanding of how encryption actually works.

Of course, I understand that judges and politicians can't be experts in every area they need to deal with. But they do have access to experts, and it's baffling to me that lawsuits and legislative attempts can go so far without anyone pointing out these fundamental flaws.
